readAloud.text: Urban green spaces provide far more than aesthetic value to city residents. Research conducted across several metropolitan areas has demonstrated that access to parks and gardens significantly reduces stress levels, encourages physical activity, and strengthens community ties. Consequently, many city councils now require developers to include public greenery in all new residential projects.

The printing press, invented by Johannes Gutenberg in the fifteenth century, revolutionised the spread of information throughout Europe. Before its invention, books were copied by hand, a slow and expensive process that limited literacy to the wealthy elite. Within fifty years of the press's introduction, millions of books had been produced, transforming education, science, and religion.

Marine biologists have observed that coral reefs support approximately a quarter of all ocean species, despite covering less than one percent of the sea floor. These delicate ecosystems are highly sensitive to changes in water temperature and acidity. When conditions become unfavourable, corals expel the algae living within their tissues, a phenomenon known as bleaching.

Universities increasingly collaborate with industry partners to ensure that graduates possess skills relevant to the modern workforce. Such partnerships allow students to undertake internships, work on real commercial projects, and build professional networks before completing their degrees. Employers, in turn, gain early access to talented graduates who already understand their organisations.

Honey bees communicate the location of food sources through a remarkable behaviour known as the waggle dance. By moving in a precise figure-eight pattern, a returning forager conveys both the direction and the distance of flowers relative to the position of the sun. This sophisticated system allows the colony to exploit resources efficiently across a wide area.

Renewable energy capacity has grown dramatically over the past decade, driven by falling costs and government incentives. Solar panels, once prohibitively expensive for households, are now among the cheapest sources of electricity in many regions. Nevertheless, the intermittent nature of wind and solar power continues to pose challenges for grid operators.

Sleep plays a crucial role in consolidating memories and processing emotional experiences. During deep sleep, the brain replays the day's events, transferring important information from short-term to long-term storage. Chronic sleep deprivation, therefore, does not merely cause tiredness; it impairs learning, decision-making, and mental health in measurable ways.

retellLecture.title: The history of timekeeping
retellLecture.sample: The lecture discussed how humans have measured time throughout history. The speaker explained that early civilisations used sundials and water clocks, which were inaccurate and impractical at night. Mechanical clocks appeared in medieval Europe, and the pendulum clock of 1656 greatly improved accuracy. Finally, the speaker noted that modern atomic clocks are so precise they lose less than a second over millions of years.
retellLecture.text: Throughout history, humans have devised increasingly accurate ways to measure time. Ancient civilisations relied on the movement of the sun, using sundials to divide the day into parts, while water clocks measured hours by the steady dripping of water from one vessel to another. These methods, however, were unreliable on cloudy days or during the night. The first mechanical clocks appeared in European monasteries in the late thirteenth century, driven by weights and gears rather than sunlight. A major breakthrough came in 1656, when Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, which was accurate to within a minute a day. Today, atomic clocks define the international standard, losing less than one second over tens of millions of years, and they underpin technologies such as GPS navigation and high-frequency financial trading.

retellLecture.title: Why cities are warmer than the countryside
retellLecture.sample: The lecture explained the urban heat island effect, meaning cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas. The speaker gave two main reasons: dark surfaces like asphalt absorb sunlight, and waste heat comes from vehicles and air conditioners. The speaker also mentioned consequences such as higher energy use and health risks, and suggested solutions including green roofs and planting more trees.
retellLecture.text: Scientists use the term urban heat island to describe the fact that cities are consistently warmer than the countryside around them, sometimes by as much as seven degrees Celsius at night. There are two principal causes. First, building materials such as asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly overnight, whereas vegetation cools the land through evaporation. Second, cities generate their own heat: cars, factories, and millions of air conditioners all pump warmth into the streets. The consequences are serious. Higher temperatures increase energy demand for cooling, worsen air pollution, and raise the risk of heat-related illness during summer. To combat the effect, many cities are now painting roofs white, planting street trees, and creating green roofs that insulate buildings and cool the surrounding air.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Should the university extend library opening hours to 24/7?
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The students discussed whether the library should open around the clock. Speaker A supported the idea because many students study late and commuter students need flexible access. Speaker B raised concerns about the cost of staffing and security at night, suggesting extended hours only during exam periods. Speaker C proposed a compromise: keeping one floor open all night with student-card entry. Overall, they agreed that longer hours were needed but disagreed about how to fund them.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I honestly think the library should be open twenty-four hours. A lot of us study best late at night, and students who commute or work part-time jobs can't always come during normal hours. Other universities already do this, so why can't we?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I see your point, but somebody has to pay for it. Overnight staffing, heating, security — that costs a lot of money, and it might mean higher fees. I'd rather see extended hours just during the exam period, when demand is genuinely high, instead of all year round.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That's fair, but demand is high all semester for some courses. Medical and engineering students basically live in the library.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Maybe there's a middle ground. We could keep just one floor open overnight with student card entry, so there's no need for extra staff at the desk. A few universities use security cameras plus card access, and it seems to work. That would cut the cost a lot.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That actually sounds reasonable. If it's limited to one floor, the cost would be much lower, and we could trial it for a semester.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I'd be happy with that as a first step, as long as the trial includes the quiet study zones.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I'm completely in favour of the ban. The city centre is choked with traffic, the air quality is terrible, and pedestrians are constantly dodging cars. European cities that have done this are now much more pleasant places to live and shop.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: That's exactly what happened in my hometown — they built park-and-ride car parks on the edge of the centre with cheap shuttle buses every ten minutes. Once people saw it was convenient, most of them stopped driving in.

turns.speaker: A

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Electric vehicles are often praised as a solution to urban air pollution, and it is true that they produce no exhaust emissions while driving. However, a complete assessment of their environmental impact must consider the entire life cycle of the vehicle. Manufacturing an electric car, particularly its lithium-ion battery, generates substantially more carbon dioxide than manufacturing a conventional petrol car, mainly because extracting and refining lithium, cobalt, and nickel is energy-intensive. Whether an electric vehicle ultimately produces fewer emissions than a petrol equivalent depends largely on how the electricity used to charge it is generated. In countries whose grids rely heavily on coal, an electric car may need to be driven for many years before its lifetime emissions fall below those of a petrol car; in countries with abundant hydroelectric or nuclear power, the break-even point arrives much sooner. Furthermore, as battery recycling improves and electricity grids continue to decarbonise, the environmental advantage of electric vehicles is expected to grow steadily over the coming decades.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Although electric vehicles produce no exhaust emissions, their overall environmental benefit depends on the carbon-intensive battery manufacturing process and the source of electricity used for charging, meaning they deliver the greatest advantage in countries with clean power grids, an advantage that will grow as grids decarbonise and battery recycling improves.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: For most of human history, people acquired language simply by growing up surrounded by it, and the question of how adults should learn a second language received little systematic attention. In the twentieth century, however, researchers began to compare different teaching methods, and their findings challenged long-held assumptions. Studies of immersion programmes, in which students are taught all subjects through the new language, showed that learners developed stronger comprehension skills than those taught grammar rules in isolation, though their writing often retained persistent errors. Later research emphasised the importance of noticing: learners improve fastest when they receive feedback that highlights the gap between their own output and accurate forms. Motivation, too, proved decisive, but not always in the expected direction; adults learning a language for immediate practical needs, such as employment, frequently outperformed those studying for examinations. Modern approaches therefore combine meaningful communication, explicit feedback, and opportunities to use the language for genuine purposes.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Twentieth-century research into second language learning found that immersion develops strong comprehension but leaves writing errors, that explicit feedback helps learners notice the gap between their output and accurate language, and that practical motivation drives faster progress, leading modern teaching to combine communication, feedback and purposeful use.

summarizeSpokenText.title: The benefits and limits of bilingualism
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The speaker discussed the advantages of bilingualism, explaining that bilingual children often develop better concentration and problem-solving skills because switching between languages exercises the brain. The speaker also noted that bilingualism may delay the symptoms of dementia in old age. However, the lecture emphasised that these benefits depend on regular use of both languages, and that claims about bilingualism raising general intelligence are exaggerated.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: For many years, researchers have studied whether speaking two languages benefits the brain, and the evidence is largely positive. Bilingual children constantly switch between their languages, and this mental juggling appears to strengthen the brain's control systems. As a result, bilinguals often perform better on tasks that require concentration and ignoring distractions. Perhaps most strikingly, studies have found that bilingual patients develop the symptoms of dementia an average of four to five years later than patients who speak only one language. However, we should be careful not to exaggerate. There is little evidence that bilingualism raises general intelligence, and the benefits seem to depend heavily on using both languages regularly throughout life. Someone who learned a language at school and never uses it is unlikely to gain these advantages. Bilingualism is best understood as a form of lifelong mental exercise rather than a shortcut to genius.

summarizeSpokenText.title: The rise of vertical farming
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture described vertical farming, where crops are grown indoors in stacked layers under LED lighting. The speaker explained the main advantages: year-round production, much less water use, and no pesticides. However, the high energy cost of artificial lighting makes vertical farming expensive, so it is currently profitable only for high-value crops like salad leaves and herbs, not for staple foods such as wheat and rice.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Vertical farming is a method of growing crops indoors, in stacked layers, under carefully controlled conditions. Instead of sunlight, the plants receive light from LED lamps, and instead of soil, their roots sit in nutrient-rich water. This approach offers several remarkable advantages. Crops can be grown all year round, regardless of the weather outside. The systems use up to ninety-five percent less water than conventional agriculture, and because the environment is sealed, no pesticides are needed. Vertical farms can also be built in cities, cutting the distance food travels to consumers. Nevertheless, the industry faces one enormous obstacle: energy. Powering thousands of LED lights is expensive, and this cost makes vertical farming unprofitable for cheap staple crops like wheat, rice, and potatoes. For now, the technology is commercially viable mainly for high-value products such as salad leaves, herbs, and strawberries.
